To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the age-related deficit in cognitive efficiency is larger for tasks requiring high executive load, (2) the age-related slowing factor for tasks requiring high load is larger for spatial than for verbal tasks, (3) this age-related dissociation between spatial and verbal tasks cannot be attributed to differences in the degree of practice, and (4) the dissociation cannot be explained by a single "common cause" mechanism.

(1) age-related slowing in cognitive tasks is not uniform across tasks; (2) slowing varies with executive control requirements; (3) age-related slowing increases with executive control demands; and (4) age-related slowing is larger for spatial tasks than for verbal tasks, but this difference is not a function of the executive control demands.
age-related slowing is not a single, unitary phenomenon.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cognitive efficiency modes in old and young subjects.
age-related deficits on tasks that are assumed to be dependent on executive functions.
the study of age-related changes in executive control processes and the mechanisms responsible for these changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cognitive efficiency modes are preserved in old age, but the efficiency modes themselves are not.
there is no single cause of cognitive decline in old age.
age-related slowing of processing is a general effect of aging that is not limited to a specific type of task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age-related slowing is not uniform across cognitive domains and that the degree of slowing is related to executive involvement.
age-related cognitive deficits are not uniform across all tasks, but are highly dependent upon the nature of the task.
age effects on cognitive performance are not unitary and that the effects are not simply a function of task complexity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
age-related slowing is not a unitary construct and that the nature and extent of the deficit depend on task complexity and the nature of the task (verbal or visuospatial).
age-related cognitive deficits are not uniform but are instead tied to specific cognitive functions and to the degree of executive control required to perform them.
the cognitive efficiency of older adults is not a single entity, but rather a set of dissociated functions that are differentially affected by aging.
